title: The CD226 costimulatory axis in type 1 diabetes
text:
The modern era of molecular biology has revealed key variants throughout the genome that are enriched in
those who develop complex autoimmune diseases, including type 1 diabetes (T1D). Our goal is to understand
how these variants in immune checkpoints contribute to a loss of immune tolerance to pancreatic -cells, and
toward that objective, this R01 renewal application is centered on CD226, a gene encoding a costimulatory
molecule associated with T1D genetic risk and disease development. The results of this project are expected to
inform on the biological mechanisms by which CD226 signaling alters peripheral tolerance and contributes
toward disease progression, as well as provide preclinical data related to therapeutic targeting the
CD226/TIGIT/CD96:CD155/CD112 pathway to correct immune defects and restore immune tolerance.

title: Deciphering the Impact of ZNF397-deficiency in Promoting TET2-driven Epigenetic Rewiring, Lineage Plasticity, and Therapy Resistance in Prostate Cancer
text:
Resistance to current AR-targeted therapies poses a significant hurdle in treating advanced prostate cancer
(PCa), severely affecting clinical outcomes for patients battling this lethal disease. Our research has identified a
prevalent ZNF397 deficiency, observed in 25-40% of PCa patients, which propels the transition of cancer cells
from an AR-driven luminal lineage to a TET2-driven lineage plastic state, thereby fostering AR-targeted therapy
resistance. This study aims to unravel the molecular mechanism behind ZNF397-deficiency-induced lineage
plasticity and AR-targeted therapy resistance, with a goal to develop innovative therapeutic approaches to
overcome resistance and benefit patients suffering from this devastating disease.

title: Proton and hyperpolarized xenon pulmonary MRI at 0.55T
text:
This project will develop pulmonary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) methods on a novel 0.55 Tesla scanner
using both conventional proton and hyperpolarized xenon imaging. It will establish 0.55 Tesla MRI as a single
modality to regionally assess lung structure, function, and tissue properties, yielding a unique, clinically valuable
approach to detect and manage lung diseases. This proposal will promote a sustainable partnership between
the NIH and the University of Virginia to develop pulmonary MRI technology for 0.55 Tesla to make advanced
pulmonary imaging more accessible and of higher value.

title: Pre-TCR Mechanotransduction: From Biology to Structure
text: ABSTRACT – PROJECT 2 A multi-step process in the thymus programs αβ T-lineage cells to distinguish self from non-self. Two sets of receptors are involved in this thymic education, namely pre-T cell receptors (preTCRs) at the early CD4−CD8−double-negative (DN) thymocyte stage followed by αβ T cell receptors (TCRs) beginning at the CD4+CD8+double-positive (DP) thymocyte stage. Signaling through the preTCR, a CD3-associated heterodimer comprising an invariant pTα chain and a clone-specific β chain, is a critical early checkpoint in thymocyte development within the T cell lineage. PreTCRs arrayed on DN thymocytes ligate peptides bound to major histocompatibility complex molecules (pMHC) on thymic stroma as do αβ TCRs that appear on DP thymocytes but use a related yet distinct molecular docking strategy. Employing synchronized fetal thymic progenitor cultures differing in the presence or absence of pMHC on support stroma and single-cell transcriptomes, we observed that although MHC-negative stroma fosters αβ T cell differentiation, the absence of preTCR-pMHC interactions leads to deviant thymocyte transcriptional programming associated with dedifferentiation and antecedent characteristics of T cell lymphoblastic and myeloid malignancies. Compensatory upregulation of diverse MHC class Ib proteins in B2m/H2-Ab1-MHC-knockout mice partially safeguards thymocyte progression in vivo but disseminated DP thymic tumors develop with aging. Thus, beside promoting β chain repertoire broadening for subsequent αβ T cell receptor utilization, preTCR-pMHC interactions limit cellular plasticity to facilitate normal thymocyte differentiation. In Aim 1 we shall correlate preTCR-pMHC bond biophysical properties described in Project 1 required for successful navigation through the β selection checkpoint with signaling, repertoire selection and thymocyte progression using our toolbox of RNA-Seq, clonotype analyses and functional studies. In conjunction with X-ray crystallographic studies of preTCRβ-pMHC, NMR methods involving select labeling, chemical shift and structural dynamics (Core B-C) and molecular dynamics under force (MDf) (Project 3) insights on the ligand binding interface, load pathways linked to bond formation and developmental progression shall be provided. Aim 2 will utilize the computational power of Project 3 to predict various altered peptide ligands (APL) in silico to be assessed experimentally for efficacy in directing repertoire development from preTCR to TCR to foster immunoprotective influenza A virus (IAV) specificities. In Aim 3 we shall establishing a facile in vitro model system to support selection and repertoire development from HSC through to CD4SP/CD8SP thymocytes, since progression through to the SP stage is inadequate in the current in vitro epithelial system offering a complete developmental trajectory analysis with translational significance. The completion of these aims will provide a greater in-depth understanding of the role of the preTCR in T cell development, offer insights into how the preTCR pretests β chains for incorporation into the αβ TCR repertoire and biological and atomistic detailing of developmental control of thymocyte repertoire generation.

title: Roles of the glycogen synthase kinase 3 alpha isoform in Alzheimers disease pathophysiology
text:
Elucidation of the basic causes underlying cognitive impairments in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and other neuronal
diseases would facilitate the development of effective therapeutic and diagnostic strategies. This project will help
determine the roles of the signaling pathway associated with the glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) isoforms
in AD pathogenesis. The results of this work could help understand the etiology and inform the future
identification of novel therapeutic targets for AD and related dementia syndromes.

title: MAPT-targeting genome editing therapy for Alzheimer's Disease
text:
Relevance to public health:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD), one of the most common forms of dementia, affects over 55 million people worldwide in 2020. It was estimated that the number will nearly double every 20 years, reaching 139 million in 2050, according to the World Alzheimer Report. The successful completion of this research project may result in a novel and effective approach for significantly improved treatment of AD.

title: Participation in the FDA Vet-LIRN Cooperative Agreement Program to strengthen analysis of animal food or animal drug samples that may be adulterated and investigation of foodborne illness outbreaks.
text:
2 Project Narrative
 Cooperative agreement between AVDL and FDA Vet-LIRN will strengthen the food safety
 system by using AVDL's capacity and capabilities to analyze animal food or animal drug
 samples that may be adulterated and investigate animal foodborne illness outbreaks.

title: Role of calcium dependent RabGAPs in endocytic trafficking pathways
text:
Rab GTPases are key regulators of endocytic and secretory pathways, with their localization and activity
precisely controlled by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs).
This project investigates the calcium-dependent regulation of a unique subfamily of RabGAPs containing an
EF-hand calcium-sensing domain. By revealing how calcium signaling orchestrates the spatial and temporal
control of Rab GTPases and membrane trafficking, this study seeks to uncover new regulatory mechanisms
and their implications for disease pathogenesis.

title: Harnessing the repetitive genome for cancer immunotherapy
text: Therapies that disrupt immune evasion through the PD-1 or CTLA-4 pathways have shown remarkable efficacy yet fail in many patients, likely due to additional mechanisms that are yet to be defined. This proposal will investigate how epigenetic silencing of the repetitive genome drives immune escape in cancer cells, and will specifically explore the role of the epigenetic repressor, SETDB 1, in silencing transposable elements and immune genes in melanoma. A deeper understanding of these mechanisms could ultimately yield new biomarkers and epigenetic therapies capable of selectively enhancing the efficacy and scope of immunotherapy for melanoma and other cancer types.

title: Core C - Computational and Quantitative Imaging Core
text:
Computational and Quantitative Imaging (Core C)
Nearly all patients treated with surgery and radiotherapy report some degree of therapy-related side effects due
to normal tissue injury, such as xerostomia, osteoradionecrosis and difficulty swallowing, with the majority
experiencing symptoms that significantly impact quality of life. Reducing these toxicity rates requires precision
in treatment, understanding what treatment is delivered to patients, spatially and temporally linking quantitative
measurements of toxicity with the treatment delivered, and finally, harnessing this wealth of information to benefit
future patients. The innovative research proposed will further develop and deploy automated segmentation and
image processing algorithms for widespread use across diagnostic, therapeutic, and response assessment
timepoints, advance anatomical models to facilitate high precision, localized, image guided cancer therapy in the
head and neck through the development of anatomical models to incorporate 2D information into 3D/4D models,
quantify the complex volumetric changes of the patient over the treatment course, and harness deep learning
techniques to predict the toxicity risks for future patients enabling the optimization of therapeutic interventions.

title: Core Grant for Vision Research Core 2
text:
CORE 2: PATHOLOGY AND IMAGING
NARRATIVE
The goal of the Pathology and Imaging core is to enable investigators to obtain state-of-the art imaging
procedures to meet their research goals. Specifically, the module (1) provides tissue processing services for
both light and electron microscopy, (2) provides access to state-of-the art imaging equipment located in
institutional core facilities and in our Cores, (3) maintains image acquisition instruments and (4) trains eye and
vision researchers on how to use and develop novel imaging technologies for their individual and collaborative
research programs. It is also responsible for the collection and maintenance of tissue specimens and cell
lines.

title: DEVELOPING GPCR MODULATORS OF SOMATOSTATIN INTERNEURONS FOR THE TREATMENT OF OPIOID USE DISORDER
text:
Approved medications and available treatments for opioid use disorder (OUD) do not adequately address
persistent symptoms that can lead to relapse; thus, we desperately need to identify new molecular targets for
medication development. In this proposal, we will identify targets expressed by a specific subtype of neuron
within prefrontal cortex that has been implicated and regulating motivated and affective behaviors. We will use
a combination of transcriptomics, electrophysiology, pharmacology, and genetic engineering to define how
candidate targets regulate brain function and opioid use behaviors.

title: Building models and tools to integrate multiscale brain imaging and multi-omics data
text:
The project will advance the field of neuroimaging by improving the methodology for muti-modal imaging and
genomics data integration, providing predictive modeling of brain-phenotypes, and identifying important
biological mechanisms. By disseminating the developed tools and software via open sources, the project can
facilitate multi-modal brain imaging and genomics data analysis that is widely used by neuroimaging community.

title: Expanding the pool of Independent Investigators in Implementation Science in Nigeria throug h HIV research training (EXPAND)
text:
The proposed Expanding the Pool of Independent Investigators in Implementation Science in Nigeria
through HIV Research training (EXPAND Nigeria) project will focus on Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn,
Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) in the area of HIV and implementation research in Nigeria. We aim
to develop a flexible, locally-tailored research curriculum incorporating hard and soft skill-building for
postdoctoral early career investigators to attain research independence, and imparts program evaluation and
knowledge translation skills to program implementers and policymakers, for high-level impact on RMNCAH
gaps in Nigeria’s HIV program. EXPAND Nigeria’s scalable curriculum and mentoring approach address both
independent research and programmatic capacity gaps, towards attaining sustainability for HIV
research/research funding, and for high-level programmatic competencies.

title: Automatic integrated biomarkers to improve prediction of lung cancer outcomes
text:
The digitization of health records and widespread availability of tumor DNA sequencing results offer a chance to
better risk-stratify patients with implications for therapy selection, monitoring, and side effect mitigation. Here,
we will test whether multimodal, artificial intelligence pipelines improve outcome modeling over standard
predictors for patients with non-small cell lung cancer at three points: 1) Patients with localized disease at risk
for relapse following definitive therapy, 2) Patients with oligometastatic disease considering consolidative
radiotherapy, 3) Patients at risk for central nervous system disease who may benefit from MRI surveillance.

title: Biostatistics and Bioinformatics Core (Core C)
text:
BIOSTATISTICS AND BIOINFORMATICS CORE (CORE C)
Appropriate statistical analysis of data resulting from translational research is critical to the advancement and
distribution of scientific information, through which the outcome of patients with malignant gliomas will be
improved. The Biostatistics and Bioinformatics Core provides comprehensive biostatistical and bioinformatic
expertise to ensure statistical integrity and optimize data analysis for SPORE studies. The Core incorporates
sound experimental design principles in each project to enhance the interpretability of the study results, carries
out data analyses using appropriate statistical methodology, and contributes to the interpretation of results via
written reports and frequent interaction with project investigators.

title: Mechanisms of DNA helicases and their regulation
text:
Helicases are essential enzymes that unwind the strands of DNA and RNA. They are critical to maintaining the
genomes of all organisms, and defective helicase function is implicated in various human disorders. The project
will use advanced biophysical techniques to understand the mechanisms of helicases involved in repairing DNA
damage, specifically investigating how helicase interactions with DNA and with accessory proteins regulate their
functions.

title: Vesicle-mediated drug resistance of Candida albicans biofilm
text:
Narrative / Public Health Relevance
Candida frequently forms biofilms on the surface of medical devices. Both drug resistance and dissemination
due to fungal cell dispersion contribute to the high mortality linked to biofilm infections; there are no effective
drug therapies for these commonly lethal fungal infections. The proposed studies will uncover the biofilm driven
regulatory pathway and effectors that govern the extracellular vesicle delivery and assembly of the protective
matrix that permits Candida to persist and disseminate from implanted devices.

title: The impact of hearing and vestibular problems on physical function, psychosocial well-being, and survival outcomes among breast cancer survivors
text:
Whether hearing and vestibular problems affect physical function, psychosocial well-being over time, and
mortality risk specifically among breast cancer survivors remain unknown. This project will use data from a
multiethnic cohort of breast cancer survivors to assess hearing and vestibular problems and the associated
physical and psychosocial health outcomes. The information generated will inform symptom screening and
treatment, increase awareness and patient-provider discussion, and improve the health and quality of life of the
growing and aging population of breast cancer survivors in the United States.

title: Targeting retrotransposons for improved treatment of refractory childhood cancer
text:
Despite significant advances in pediatric cancer treatment, childhood cancer remains the commonest cause of
death from disease in children, due to resistance of the tumor cells to drug treatment. Our recent research has
unveiled a new mechanism of cancer drug resistance driven by virus-like components of our genome known as
“retrotransposons”. We've identified a way to block this resistance by safe drugs already used for viral diseases
and discovered that the immune system can target cells with activated retrotransposons. Our program aims to
explore these findings further, potentially offering new hope to children with currently untreatable cancers.
